## Task 2 of Multi100 {#task-2-in-the-analysts-own-words .smaller}

::: {.claimcard .small}
- produce a single, main result in terms of statistical families of z-, t-, F-, or $\chi^2$ tests (or their alternative or non-parametric versions).
- disregard contextual variables related to the EU policies and party EU salience and party EU positions indexes in your analysis.
- use the **positive non-materialist form of EU framing** in your analysis.
- use the **unemployment rate** as the measure for poor economic performance in your analysis.
:::

::: {.small}
Four instructions, quoted from my own Task 2 report. Everything else – estimator, sample, weighting, functional form, how you build the scale – was left to us.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Multi100 was designed to fix just enough to make the numbers comparable and to leave the rest free, so that what remained would be a measurement of **analytical variability itself**.
:::

::: notes
Here, word for word, is what Multi100 asked of us in its second task, copied from the report that I filed. One main result, as a z, t, F or chi-squared test. Disregard the contextual variables that concern EU policies and the salience of the EU and its position for the parties. Use the positive non-materialist form of EU framing, which the paper calls the cosmopolitan dimension. And use the unemployment rate as the measure of poor economic performance. That is the whole brief. Everything else was left open: which estimator, which sample, whether to weight, what functional form, and even how to build the scale out of the underlying items. And that is how the design was meant to work. Multi100 fixed just enough to make five numbers comparable and left the rest free, so that what remained would be a measurement of analytical variability itself rather than of anything about the paper. Everything they left open is a place where five competent people could legitimately part company, and they did.
:::

## What the instructions assume {#what-those-three-instructions-assume .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **'A single, main result'** assumes that one test statistic can stand for the claim, and leaves its degrees of freedom to the software of each analyst
- **'The positive non-materialist form'** is the cosmopolitan scale of the paper. It assumes that the five items form one scale, and that the summary used in the paper, each respondent's share of mentions, is the right one; a mean, a sum or a factor score would all be defensible
- **'The unemployment rate'** assumes that the claim is about unemployment. The abstract of the paper says "poor economic performances" – which also names GDP growth
- **'Disregard contextual variables'** of EU policy and party positions removes the variables of Model 2. Read literally, it leaves the rest of Model 1 to the analyst, yet four of the five fitted unemployment alone
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these is wrong. Each one is a **decision**, made for you, that a different study could reasonably have made differently.
:::

::: notes
Now take the instructions apart, because each rests on an assumption. Asking for a single main result assumes that one test statistic can stand for the claim, and it leaves the degrees of freedom to whatever the software of each analyst reports, which is where the conversion went wrong for one of us. The positive non-materialist form is the cosmopolitan scale, and it takes for granted that the five items – peace, democracy, freedom of movement, cultural diversity, a stronger voice in the world – form one scale, summarised as each respondent's share of mentions. A mean would be defensible, and so would a sum or a factor score. 'The unemployment rate' assumes that the claim is about unemployment, but the abstract says "poor economic performances", which just as clearly names GDP growth – and in the free task all five of us used a GDP measure, and three of us used nothing else. The last instruction removes the EU-policy and party variables of Model 2. Read literally, it leaves individual controls, growth and the education interactions to us, and four of the five dropped them all. None of these is wrong. Each is a decision, made for you, that another study could reasonably have made differently.
:::

## The EU-frames panel {#the-panel-you-will-work-on .smaller}

::: {.small}
`EUframes_cy.csv` – **270 rows**, one per country-year · 27 countries · 2004–2013

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| `cntry`, `year` | the cell |
| `mcosmo` | mean cosmopolitan framing in that country-year, 0–1 |
| `mutil`, `mcomm`, `mlib` | the other three framing scales |
| `mpos`, `mneg` | the two composites – all positive items, all negative items |
| `unemp`, `growth` | national unemployment rate and GDP growth |
| `n_cy` | how many survey respondents are behind the cell |
| `bailout` | 1 if an EU/IMF assistance programme was running |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
`n_cy` is the interesting one: cells are built from very different numbers of people, which is why **weighting** is a live choice on the menu.
:::

::: notes
Here is the panel that you looked at in Hands-on 2, now column by column, because everything from now on works from it. Two hundred and seventy rows, one per country-year, twenty-seven countries over ten years. Country and year identify the cell. Mcosmo is the mean cosmopolitan framing in that cell, on a nought-to-one scale, and the other framing scales sit beside it. Unemployment and growth are the national macro indicators. And then n underscore cy, which counts how many survey respondents are behind each cell – and that is the interesting column, because those counts differ a great deal between cells. A country-year built from two thousand respondents and one built from five hundred are not equally precise, which is why whether to weight by n is a live choice on the specification menu. It is the one data file that you will load yourself.
:::
## Analyst no. 6 {#you-are-analyst-no.-6}

::: {.big}
- Aim 1: **reproduce** analyst **C6HJR**'s constrained result
:::

  - **What Multi100 asked:** one main test result for the positive non-materialist (cosmopolitan) framing and the unemployment rate, without the contextual variables of EU policy and party positions

  - **What I submitted:** a two-way fixed-effects model, `mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year`

  - **What Multi100 recorded:** t ≈ −3.80 (df = 233, N = 270, partial *r* ≈ −0.242)

::: notes
So here is your first job as the sixth analyst, and it is the same job I had. Multi100 asked for one main result on the cosmopolitan framing and the unemployment rate, without the contextual variables of EU policy and party positions. What I submitted was a two-way fixed-effects model – cosmopolitan framing on centred unemployment, with country and year absorbed – and what Multi100 recorded for me is a t of minus three point eight zero, on two hundred and thirty-three degrees of freedom, which standardises to a partial correlation of minus point two four. Now, you have my code. You have my data. The whole of reproducibility is the question of whether that is enough for you to get my number back. Let us find out.
:::
